BABY ACTOR TO APPEAR
IN "PETE."
A very young actor--probably the youngest ever seen on any stage--will make his first appearance in a by no means unimportant part in the forthcoming production of "Pete" at the Lyceum Theatre.
The story, as set forth in "The Manxman," from which the play is adapted, tells how Kate Creggan runs away from home, her husband, Pete, and her baby, Little Phil.

The management conceived the idea of filling the part of Little Phil with a real live baby instead of the usual dummy; they had not to look far. The ideal baby was found almost at hand, and it is expected that Little Phil, only seven weeks old, will soon be the talk of all London.

During rehearsals the baby has behaved admirably, and no fears are entertained of his suffering from stage fright when the curtain goes up on the first night. His part is not a speaking one, and so far he has shown no disposition to make it a crying one. Even though he should cry a little, it will only make the scene all the more realistic.

In real life Little Phil is known as George Samuel Crocker, and through his father he has had an interest in the theatre all his life. His salary is said to be commensurate with the important part he plays, and is certainly quite out of proportion to his size.
The first performance of "Pete" takes place on August 29, when Little Phil will no doubt meet with an enthusiastic reaction.

V. FORBIN
PARIS

WEDNESDAY, JULY 8, 1914
THIS week we make our bow before the world as millionaires.

Please do not misunderstand: We have not come into a fortune. We have earned a million. Ten years of hard work, of constantly increasing and ever-varied effort, have earned it for us. And our authenticated million, which we place in its seven figures, at the head of this article, is not a million of money. It represents, roundly, the latest certified average of our daily circulation. We have reached—in fact we have passed—a million a day. We are millionaires.
We may be forgiven for pointing out, with some pride, that those figures of our daily average circulation, reached during June, 1914, constitute a record in the history of daily journalism.
Never before during normal times has a daily paper been produced—much less a daily illustrated paper—of sixteen to twenty pages in more than a million copies.

Think first and principally what it means in expense and bulk of paper—that paper, the production and preparation of which is the great technical problem of modern journalism. The paper used, on the average, for a production of more than a million copies of The Daily Mirror is nearly seventy-five tons a day.

BIRTHS AND DEATHS.

THERE is a scientific point of view of this question which it would be well to bear in mind. In both the animal and vegetable kingdoms we find that plenty or poverty on the part of the parents and safety or danger to the offspring are in some way closely connected with rapidity of increase or the reverse.

This fact is well understood and carefully acted upon by the fruit or flower grower, and he systematically restricts the plant's food, not, indeed, by cutting off the supply of that food, which is in the air all around it, but by decreasing the number of the plant's mouths, the "stomata" which cover the leaves; in other words, he prunes the tree. The life of the tree is reduced from opulence to comparative poverty.

"Luxury - Lovers" Who Will Not Marry on £3 a Week.

THE letter signed "B. L.," advocating £3 a week marriages, interested me very much. I am quite in agreement with him in his scathing scorn of the young man who "would not dream" of marrying with an income of less than £500 a year.

I think these pampered bachelors are made what they are by the influence of certain charming-luxury-loving girl friends who have a false perspective of life, and whose one aim and object is to have a good time at any cost.

I mentioned the idea of a £3 a week marriage to a girl friend of mine. She laughed scornfully.

"How impossible, how absurd!" she cried. "Why, it would be impossible to have any fun or any luxuries at all." "Yes," I gently remarked, "but you would have your husband, the duties of keeping your little home in order, occasionally entertaining your friends would not be out of the question, and you could have charming little outings together."
"But I should never be able to go to dances and dinners, and I should never be able to afford a new dress or a new hat," she cried, somewhat Pettishly.
"Oh, you selfish little woman!" I said—I know her sufficiently well to say these things—"isn't it the best fun of all to sacrifice needless luxuries and pleasures for the sake of the man you love?"

I can imagine how indigenous the thousands of young men are who married on less than £2 a week at the twaddle of people who are "horried" at the idea of £3 a week marriages. I should like to hear their private remarks on the question. ECONOMICAL.

A flame of colour burned for a moment in the girl's cheeks as she stood there alone in the quiet of the blue and white bedroom, the room that was fragrant with all her delicate hopes and girlish secrets.
As she stood there words long since read and forgotten floated to the surface of her memory: "Love blows as the wind blows...."

Love blows into my heart like the wind. . . " It was so that this love had blown into her heart—on the wings of a strong and purifying wind, which had swept shams and unrealities and falsehood scattering before it.
There was a very tender light in Pamela Chetwynd's eyes as she obeyed the summons of the maid who told her that Mrs. Wilmington's car was waiting at the door.

Mrs. Wilmington was a small, delicately pretty old lady, who had presented Pamela at Court, and, as a rule, acted as her chaperon unless the girl went, as she sometimes did, with Lydia Hatteras, under Mrs. Milward's wing.

She greeted Pamela affectionately, and made some charmingly graceful remark about her gown, then relapsed again into her semi-slumbers in the corner of the luxurious landaulette. Pamela was not sorry for that; she had her own dreams to occupy her mind.

The car stopped before the brilliantly-illuminated house, with its crowds and its awnings, and Pamela's heart beat a little quickly as she passed up the great thronged staircase. Her eyes searched restlessly for the one familiar face she desired to see, so restlessly that there was more than one sore heart in the crowd whose greeting had been passed by.

As she passed into the great ballroom after the usual perfunctory greetings with her hostess, a small, charmingly manned, but already fatigued lady, whose hand ached with the mechanical exercise of several hundred handshakes, Pamela Chetwynd was conscious of a little thrill of disappointment.
Jack Selwyn was not there. It was unreasonable, of course, she recognised that, yet she had expected to find him there waiting....

WHAT DO THEY CARE?

THE papers have contained an unusual amount of grown-up criticism of infants lately—criticism of those not legally entitled to speak for themselves. Schoolboys seldom take the trouble to write letters to anybody, still less to reply to the criticism of the outer world; and so that world seldom gets to hear their point of view. Gradually it comes to be supposed that the boy's point of view is something very mysterious, and subversive, like an anarchist's.
It is something vaguely suspected as being opposite to the adult attitude.

Its opposition is displayed by the fact that nothing the grown-ups say makes the smallest difference to the boy; unless enforced upon him, which nowadays seldom happens; boys being allowed to do very much as they like. Criticism unaccompanied by the physical argument falls upon them in vain.

Each of 700 Tourists to Try to Induce One Britisher to Emigrate.

OTTAWA, Wednesday.—A party of 700 excursionists will sail from Montreal to-morrow by the Canadian Northern steamer Royal George, for a tour of the British Isles under the auspices of the "Sons of England."
Each member of the party will try to induce one resident of Great Britain to come to Canada.
The passenger traffic on the Canadian steamship lines this summer is the largest for many years.

Two thousand two hundred and twelve tourists will leave Montreal this week, and every berth on the boats of the Allan Line for first and second class passengers is reserved for the six weeks beginning on August 15.—Reuter.
FIRE ON EXCURSION STEAMER.

NEW YORK, Wednesday.—Two hundred passengers, who were returning to New York from Rockaway Reach, a popular seaside resort in New York State, on board the steamer Grand Republic, were badly scared by a fire which broke out amidships while the ship was entering the Narrows.
The steamboat was turned and made fast to the pier of the Crescent Athletic Club, and all were got off safely.—Reuter.

"Lost, are you?" said a kindly policeman on Hampstead Heath yesterday to a very small boy who was endeavouring to stay his tears by trying to screw both his fists into his eyes. "Then come with me," continued the policeman, who led his newly-found charge to a tent which is erected specially on Bank Holiday for the benefit of small mortals who have strayed from their parents. On arrival at the tent the

yongsters are made as happy as possible. Their names and addresses are ascertained, and if not applied for by dusk they are taken to the police-station, and their parents are communicated with.
